subject: Arabic
source: Drive: Curriculum/Arabic folder and Secondary Lesson Plan - Arabic - Y8 (format and approach); Madinah-style progression (al-, sun and moon letters, prepositions); National Curriculum KS2 languages

lessons.title: The: using al-
objectives: Add ال to a noun to say 'the'
Read definite nouns with correct vowels
starter: Say 'my book' and 'my bag' in Arabic.
Say 'this is a big house' in Arabic.
How do you ask 'whose is this?' in Arabic?

teach.heading: A book and the book
teach.note: Hold up one book and say 'a book'. Then point to the specific book and say 'the book'. Show how al- joins to the front of the word. Ask pupils where it is written: right side, the start of the word.

teach.heading: Dropping the -n sound
teach.note: Explain that with al- we remove the double mark of -un (tanween) and use a single mark. Do not discuss grammar terms; say 'two marks become one'. Pupils copy the change on mini whiteboards.

teach.heading: The ... is ...
teach.note: Contrast: بَيْتٌ كَبِيرٌ (a big house) vs الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ (the house is big). With al-, the sentence says 'the ... is ...'. Show the difference with colour coding. This is a key point and a common error.

teach.heading: Girl words with al-
teach.note: Use feminine examples. Pupils say each sentence and translate. Ask: why is it jameela not jameel? (hadeeqa is a girl word). Praise correct agreement.

teach.heading: Say it, spot it
teach.note: Flash words quickly; pupils say 'the' if it has al-. Then flash sentences and pupils translate. End by reading all sentences together.

practice: Say 'this is my bag' in Arabic.
Turn a book / a house / a mosque into 'the book / the house / the mosque'.
Say 'the garden is beautiful' in Arabic.
independent: Write 'the' forms of: بَاب / نَافِذَة / كُرْسِي / طَاوِلَة.
Write three 'the ... is ...' sentences with adjectives.
Draw a house and label with al-: الْبَابُ، النَّافِذَةُ، ...
exit: Say 'the mosque is big' in Arabic.
lessons.homework: Write five sentences starting with 'al-' about things in your home.
lessons.send: SEND: highlight al- in colour, use sentence strips. EAL: compare with 'the' in home language. Stretch: write four sentences linking two nouns with wa (e.g. الْبَابُ كَبِيرٌ وَالنَّافِذَةُ صَغِيرَةٌ).

lessons.title: Sun letters and moon letters
objectives: Pronounce al- correctly before sun and moon letters
Sort words into sun and moon groups
Read words such as ash-shams and al-qamar

keywords.def: a mark that doubles a sound

starter: Say 'the book' and 'the mosque' in Arabic.
Say 'the room is small' in Arabic.
What does the ending ـةٌ show?

teach.heading: Two ways to say al-
bullets: The l is said or silent
teach.note: Say both words. Ask: do you hear the 'l' in al-qamar? (yes). Do you hear 'l' in ash-shams? (no). This is the difference. Show the shadda over the first letter in ash-shams.

teach.heading: Moon letters
teach.note: Teach: moon letters include ب ج ح خ ع غ ف ق ك م ه و ي and hamza/alif. You can say: if you hear the 'l' it is a moon letter. Do not require them to memorise all letters, but give 'baa, jeem, Haa, khaa, meem, qaaf, kaaf' as examples.

teach.heading: Sun letters
teach.note: Teach: the l changes to match the next letter, which is doubled. Examples: ش س ن ت ط د ر ز ص ض ظ ث ذ ل. Make a mnemonic: sun letters are 'hot' and melt the l. Pupils repeat as-sayyaara, an-naafidha, at-taawila.

teach.heading: Sort the words
teach.note: Use a two-column sorting task on screen. Pupils drag or call out which group. Check by reading aloud. Misconception: that spelling changes; it doesn't - only the pronunciation changes.

teach.heading: Listen and say
teach.note: Play a listening game: read words aloud; pupils shout 'shams' or 'qamar'. Then reverse: show the word, pupils read it. Keep pace brisk and fun.

practice: Turn these into 'the ...': bayt, qalam, hadeeqa.
Translate 'the garden is beautiful' into English.
Sort 10 words into sun and moon groups.
Read aloud ten words and say whether the l is heard.
independent: Sort: الْقَلَمُ، السَّيَّارَةُ، الْبَابُ، النَّافِذَةُ، الْمَسْجِدُ، الطَّاوِلَةُ.
Write the transliteration of each word with the right sound.
Make three sentences using words from each group.
exit: Is 'ash-shams' a sun or moon word?
lessons.homework: Find five Arabic words with al- at home or online and decide if each is sun or moon.
lessons.send: SEND: colour-code sun and moon words and provide audio support. EAL: practise saying the doubled sound slowly. Stretch: find a rule for which letters are sun letters, using tongue position.

lessons.title: Days of the week
objectives: Say the seven days in Arabic
starter: Say 'the moon' and 'the sun' in Arabic.
Is 'as-sayyaara' a sun or moon word?
How do you say 'the mosque is beautiful' in Arabic?

teach.heading: Days of the week
teach.note: Say the first three days with a rhythm and clapping. Link to numbers: ahad = one, ithnayn = two, thulaathaa' = three. Pupils recall numbers 1 to 3.

teach.heading: More days
teach.note: arbi'aa' = four, khamees = five. Jumu'a connects to gathering. Mention Surah al-Jumu'ah 62:9 as the Qur'an's mention of the call to the Friday prayer, in simple words. Ask: what do you do on Fridays?

teach.heading: The week
teach.note: Say all seven days in order from Sunday. Repeat as a chant. Misconception: the Arabic week starts on Sunday in many Arab countries; in the UK we often start on Monday. Compare.

teach.heading: What day is today?
teach.note: Model the question and answer. Ask pupils to answer for today (the lesson day). Draw a calendar on screen and have pupils point to the day. Practise in pairs.

teach.heading: Days and activities
teach.note: Optional extension: link days with activities in Arabic, e.g. 'On Friday I pray in the mosque'. Keep simple; most pupils practise the days. Reinforce with songs or chants.

practice: Count from one to five in Arabic.
Say 'the mosque is big' in Arabic.
Is 'al-qamar' a sun or moon word?
Order the seven days on a calendar.
Ask and answer 'maa l-yawm?' for different days.
independent: Make a weekly timetable with the Arabic day names.
exit: How do you ask 'What day is it today?' in Arabic?
lessons.homework: Learn the days in order and perform the chant to someone at home.
lessons.send: SEND: visual timetable with colour for each day; chant with actions. EAL: write the days in the home language beside the Arabic. Stretch: write sentences about what you do on three days.

lessons.title: Where is it? in, on, under
objectives: Use fee, 'alaa and tahta to describe position
Write short sentences about where things are
starter: Say the days of the week in order.

teach.heading: Where?
teach.note: Hide a pen and ask 'ayna l-qalam?' Pupils search and answer. Introduce the question word with gestures. Practise the sound 'ay' as in 'eye'.

teach.heading: In, on, under
teach.note: Use real objects: the book in the bag, on the table, under the chair. Say each phrase with an action. Pupils copy. Mention that 'alaa starts with the ع sound from the throat; use a gentle voice.

teach.heading: The sentence
teach.note: Read the sentences. Point out that after fee, 'alaa, tahta the noun ending changes to -i (kasra). Say 'the little line goes under'. Do not teach case names; just show the pattern.

teach.heading: Next to
bullets: The mosque is next to the house
teach.note: Introduce bi-jaanibi using a picture of a street. Pupils say where the mosque, house and school are. Ask about the neighbourhood.

teach.heading: Question and answer
teach.note: Pupils work in pairs with a picture scene. One asks ayna, the other answers. Rotate after two minutes. Teacher listens and notes common errors.

practice: Say the days of the week in Arabic.
Describe where three objects are in the picture.
Hide an object and ask your partner to find it with 'ayna'.
independent: Write four sentences about the position of objects in your room.
Draw a room and label with fee/'alaa/tahta.
exit: How do you say 'under' in Arabic?
Say 'the book is on the table' in Arabic.
lessons.homework: Write three sentences about where three things are in your home.
lessons.send: SEND: use real objects and drag-and-drop prepositions. EAL: label objects in two languages. Stretch: write a short description of a street with five places using bi-jaanibi.
